nodes.name: Matched data from files A and B
nodes.statement: To setup the problem more concretely, suppose the data $(y_1,\mathbf{x}_1),\ldots, (y_n,\mathbf{x}_n)$ is obtained from matching two data files $A$ and $B$, where for each $i$, $y_i\in\mathbb{R}$ resides in file $A$ and $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ resides in file $B$.

nodes.name: Sparsely permuted linear regression model
nodes.statement: If the number of such mismatches is known to be less than or equal to $k\le n$, then there is an unknown permutation $\varphi$ on $[n] \coloneq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ so that: $\varphi$ moves at most $k$ of the indices, and $(y_1,\mathbf{x}_{\varphi(1)}),\ldots,(y_n,\mathbf{x}_{\varphi(n)}) $ are independent realizations from the classical linear regression model \begin{equation} y=\mathbf{x}^\top\beta^* +\epsilon, \: \text{where $\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and $\mathbf{x}\perp\!\!\!\perp\epsilon$.} \end{equation}
differentia: $\varphi$ moves at most $k$ of the indices
nodes.statement_short: Responses are matched to predictors by an unknown permutation $\varphi$ moving at most $k$ indices, under a Gaussian linear model.

nodes.name: Classical linear regression model
nodes.statement: y=\mathbf{x}^\top\beta^* +\epsilon, \: \text{where $\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and $\mathbf{x}\perp\!\!\!\perp\epsilon$.}
nodes.label: eq:lr

nodes.name: Permutation matrix $\Pi^*$ and design matrix $X$
nodes.statement: Let $\Pi^*$ and $\Pi^{*\T}$ be the matrix representations of $\varphi$ and its inverse, respectively, and let $X^\top=\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{x}_1&\cdots&\mathbf{x}_d\end{pmatrix}$.

nodes.name: Permuted regression model in matrix form
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \mathbf{y} &=\Pi^*X\beta^* +\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\: \text{where $\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top$ and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n)^\top$} \\ \Leftrightarrow \; \Pi^{*\T} \mathbf{y} &= X\beta^* + \Pi^{*\T} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}. \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:lrwp

nodes.name: Hamming distance between permutation matrices
nodes.statement: Let us consider the number of mismatches which can be expressed as $d_H(\Pi^*,I_n)\coloneq|\{ i:\: \Pi_{ii}^*=0\}|$, the Hamming distance between $\Pi^*$ and the identity matrix $I_n$.

nodes.name: Hamming-constrained least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*,\beta^*)$
nodes.statement: We can naturally estimate $\Pi^*$ and $\beta^*$ by a least-squares approach as: \begin{align} \begin{split} (\widehat{\Pi},\wh{\beta})=\argmin_{\Pi,\beta} \:& \: \|\Pi X\beta-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2\\ \text{subject to}\: &\: d_H(\Pi,I_n)\le k, \end{split} \end{align} where $\Pi$ and $\beta$ run over $\mathcal{P}_n$, the set of all permutation matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, and $\mathbb{R}^d$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Jointly minimize the squared residual over permutations within Hamming distance $k$ of identity and regression vectors.

nodes.name: Least squares estimator over k-sparse permutations
nodes.statement: \begin{split} (\widehat{\Pi},\wh{\beta})=\argmin_{\Pi,\beta} \:& \: \|\Pi X\beta-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2\\ \text{subject to}\: &\: d_H(\Pi,I_n)\le k, \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:lsq

nodes.name: k-sparse permutation
nodes.statement: A permutation respectively its matrix representation $\Pi$ is said to be $k$-sparse if $d_H(\Pi, I_n)\le k$.

nodes.name: NP-hardness of least squares with unknown permutation
nodes.statement: We note that \cite{Pananjady2016} have shown that unless $d=1$ the optimization problem \eqref{eq:lsq} is NP-hard for $k=n$.

nodes.name: NP-hardness for k a fraction of n
nodes.statement: The same is true for any $k$ that is defined as a fraction of $n$.
assumptions: any $k$ that is defined as a fraction of $n$

nodes.name: Identity matrix and unit sphere notation
nodes.statement: For a positive integer $m$, $I_m$ denotes the $m \times m$ identity matrix, and $\mathbb{S}^{m-1}$ denotes the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^m$.

nodes.name: Cardinality notation
nodes.statement: We write $|S|$ for the cardinality of a set $S$.

nodes.name: Set complement notation
nodes.statement: The complement of $S$ with respect to a given base set depending on the context is denoted by $S^c$.

nodes.name: Spectral norm and column space
nodes.statement: For a matrix $A$, $\nnorm{A}_2 = \sigma_{\max}(A)$ denotes its spectral norm respectively maximum singular value, and $\text{range}(A)$ denotes the column space of $A$.

nodes.name: Subvector notation
nodes.statement: For an index set $I \subseteq [m] \coloneq \{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $v \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $v_{I}$ denotes the subvector of $v$ corresponding to $I$.

nodes.name: Maximum notation $a \vee b$
nodes.statement: We write $a \vee b = \max\{a,b\}$.

nodes.name: Generic positive constants
nodes.statement: Positive constants are denoted by $C$, $c$, $c_1$ etc.

nodes.name: Big-O notation
nodes.statement: We make use of the usual Big-O notation in terms of $O$, $o$, $\Omega$ and $\Theta$.

nodes.name: Bias of OLS under matching error (Neter et al.)
nodes.statement: Early work in \cite{Neter65} recognizes the adverse effect of matching error on the regression analysis of linked datasets. They show that as a consequence of matching error, the ordinary least squares estimator $\wh{\beta}^{\text{ols}}$ is generally not an unbiased estimator of $\beta^*$.
conclusions: the ordinary least squares estimator $\wh{\beta}^{\text{ols}}$ is generally not an unbiased estimator of $\beta^*$
assumptions: as a consequence of matching error

nodes.name: Random matching model of Neter et al.
nodes.statement: Letting $z_i$ denote the response that is actually in correspondence to $\mathbf{x}_i$, and letting $y_i$ denote the response that has been matched to $\mathbf{x}_i$, the model in \cite{Neter65} assumes that for $i=1,\ldots,n$, \begin{equation} y_i=\begin{cases} z_i&\text{with probability $q_{ii}$}\\ z_j&\text{with probability $q_{ij}, \; i \neq j$}. \end{cases} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Random matching probabilities
nodes.statement: y_i=\begin{cases} z_i&\text{with probability $q_{ii}$}\\ z_j&\text{with probability $q_{ij}, \; i \neq j$}. \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq:yz

nodes.name: Broken sample
nodes.statement: A broken sample is a sample of $(y_i, \mathbf{x}_i)$-pairs that up to some permutation of the $\{\mathbf{x}_i\}$ (or equivalently the $\{ y_i \}$) are generated from their joint distribution.
differentia: up to some permutation of the $\{\mathbf{x}_i\}$ (or equivalently the $\{ y_i \}$) are generated from their joint distribution

nodes.name: Gaussian design (G)
nodes.statement: In the sequel, unless stated otherwise, we assume Gaussian design for the $\{ \mathbf{x}_i \}_{i = 1}^n$: \begin{equation*} (\text{\textbf{G}}): \qquad \mathbf{x}_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} N(0, I_d), \; \; i \in [n]. \end{equation*}
also_stated_at: The analysis in this paper concerns estimators of $\Pi^*$ and $\beta^*$ given model \eqref{eq:lr} under the additional assumption $\mathbf{x}_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} N(0, I_d)$, $i \in [n]$, as also assumed in the recent work \cite{Pananjady2016}.

nodes.name: Extension to correlated Gaussian design
nodes.statement: Our results generalize to the case $ \mathbf{x}_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} N(0, \Sigma), \; i \in [n]$, for a symmetric positive definite matrix $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ in a straightforward manner by defining a new regression parameter $\Sigma^{1/2} \beta^*$. An estimator of that parameter (as discussed in the sequel) and an estimator of $\Sigma$ can then be combined to form an estimator of $\beta^*$. Note that estimation of $\Sigma$ is not affected by the presence of an unknown permutation.
nodes.statement_short: Results extend to $N(0,\Sigma)$ design by estimating $\Sigma^{1/2}\beta^*$ and $\Sigma$ separately.

nodes.name: Inconsistency of unconstrained least squares
nodes.statement: Let $\beta^* = 0$ and $\Pi^* = I_n$, i.e., $\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$ and consider the estimator \eqref{eq:lsq} with $k = n$. Then there exist constants $c,C > 0$ such that with probability at least $1 - C \exp(-c n)$ \begin{equation*} \nnorm{\wh{\beta}}_2^2 \geq \frac{n}{2n + d}\frac{\sigma^2}{32\pi^2}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints:\\ a negative result
conclusions: there exist constants $c,C > 0$ such that with probability at least $1 - C \exp(-c n)$ \begin{equation*} \nnorm{\wh{\beta}}_2^2 \geq \frac{n}{2n + d}\frac{\sigma^2}{32\pi^2}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: With no constraint on the permutation, least squares overfits pure noise: $\|\hat\beta\|_2^2$ stays bounded below w.h.p.
nodes.label: prop:negative_result

nodes.name: Interpretation of the negative result
nodes.statement: In other words, in a pure noise setting, $\nnorm{\wh{\beta}}_2$ will be bounded away from zero by a constant (assuming $d = O(n)$).
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints:\\ a negative result

nodes.name: Inconsistency of least squares for d=1 (Abid et al.)
nodes.statement: A result of a similar flavor is shown in \cite{Abid2017}. For $d = 1$, they show that the estimator $\wh{\beta}$ converges almost surely to a limit different from $\beta^*$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$, and they derive an explicit expression for that limit.
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints:\\ a negative result
conclusions: the estimator $\wh{\beta}$ converges almost surely to a limit different from $\beta^*$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$

nodes.name: Minimax lower bound for denoising with arbitrary permutation (Pananjady et al.)
nodes.statement: Theorem 1 in \cite{Pananjady2017} indicates that the answer is negative: they show that for any estimator $(\wt{\Pi}, \wt{\beta})$, one has \begin{equation*} \sup_{\Pi^* \in \mc{P}_n, \; \beta^* \in \mathbb{R}^d} \E\left[\textstyle\frac{1}{n} \nnorm{\wt{\Pi} X \wt{\beta} - \Pi^* X \beta^*}_2^2\right] \geq c \sigma^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints:\\ a negative result

nodes.name: SNR lower bound for estimating beta (Hsu et al.)
nodes.statement: Along this direction, another negative result is shown in \cite{Hsu2017}. They demonstrate that a lower bound on the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) \begin{equation} \text{SNR} = \nnorm{\beta^*}_2^2 / \sigma^2 \end{equation} of the order $\Omega(d / \log \log n)$ is required for any estimator of $\beta^*$ to achieve a non-trivial expected relative estimation error\footnote{Non-trivial here refers to a relative estimation error of lower order than that of the estimator $\wh{\theta} \equiv 0$.}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints:\\ a negative result
conclusions: of the order $\Omega(d / \log \log n)$ is required for any estimator of $\beta^*$ to achieve a non-trivial expected relative estimation error

nodes.name: Signal-to-noise ratio
nodes.statement: \text{SNR} = \nnorm{\beta^*}_2^2 / \sigma^2
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints:\\ a negative result
nodes.label: eq:snr

nodes.name: Permutation recovery by least squares at polynomial SNR (Pananjady et al.)
nodes.statement: As shown in \cite{Pananjady2016}, the condition $\text{SNR} > n^c$ for $c$ large enough is sufficient for the solution $\wh{\Pi}$ of \eqref{eq:lsq} to recover $\Pi^*$, in which case $\nnorm{\wh{\beta} - \beta^*}_2^2$ scales as $O(d/n)$ as in the usual regression setting in the absence of an unknown permutation.
nodes.section: 2.1 Least squares estimation of $(\Pi^*, \beta^*)$ without additional constraints:\\ a negative result
assumptions: the condition $\text{SNR} > n^c$ for $c$ large enough
conclusions: is sufficient for the solution $\wh{\Pi}$ of \eqref{eq:lsq} to recover $\Pi^*$
also_stated_at: This is to be compared to a result in \cite{Pananjady2016} stating that the estimator $\wh{\Pi}$ in \eqref{eq:lsq} recovers $\Pi^*$ if $\text{SNR} = \Omega(n^c)$, where the constant $c > 0$ is not specified.

nodes.name: Set of k-sparse permutation matrices $\mc{P}_{n,k}$
nodes.statement: For $0 \leq k \leq n$, let us introduce the shorthand \begin{equation*} \mc{P}_{n, k} = \{\Pi \in \mc{P}_n:\; d_H(\Pi,I_n)\le k \} \end{equation*} for the constraint set of $\Pi$ in problem \eqref{eq:lsq}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$

nodes.name: Gaussian width
nodes.statement: Moreover, for a compact and symmetric\footnote{A set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is called symmetric if $x \in S$ implies that $-x \in S$.} set $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, its Gaussian width is defined by \begin{equation} w(K) = \E\nolimits_{g \sim N(0, I_n)}\left[\sup_{x \in K} |\scp{g}{x}| \right]. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian width $w(K)$: expected supremum of $|\langle g,x\rangle|$ over $x\in K$ for standard Gaussian $g$.

nodes.name: Gaussian width
nodes.statement: w(K) = \E\nolimits_{g \sim N(0, I_n)}\left[\sup_{x \in K} |\scp{g}{x}| \right].
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$
nodes.label: eq:gaussianwidth

nodes.name: Set $\mc{T}$ of normalized permutation differences
nodes.statement: In our setting, we use the Gaussian width \eqref{eq:gaussianwidth} in conjunction with the set \begin{equation} \mc{T} = \bigcup_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \left\{\text{range}(\Pi - \Pi^{*\T}) \right\} \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, \end{equation} where we recall that $\Pi^{*\T} \in \mc{P}_{n,k}$ is the inverse of $\Pi^*$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$

nodes.name: Set T
nodes.statement: \mc{T} = \bigcup_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \left\{\text{range}(\Pi - \Pi^{*\T}) \right\} \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1},
nodes.section: 2.2 Least squares estimation of $\beta^*$ if $\Pi^*$ is $k$-sparse, $k \ll n$
nodes.label: eq:setT

nodes.name: Interpretation of the sample size condition
nodes.statement: We start our interpretation of Theorem \ref{theo:constrained_permutation} by inspecting condition \eqref{eq:cond_samples_unrelaxed} which imposes a limit on how large $d$ and $k$ can be in relation to $n$. Roughly speaking, the requirements are $n = \Omega(d)$ and $n = \Omega(w^2(\mc{T}))$. In light of \eqref{eq:bound_width_T}, the latter condition becomes $n = \Omega(k \log(n/k))$. Specifically, let us fix $\varepsilon = 1/4$ and $d = \alpha n$ for $\alpha \in (0,\frac{1}{4})$, then \eqref{eq:cond_samples_unrelaxed} essentially evaluates as \begin{equation*} n \geq \left(\frac{8}{3 (\sqrt{1 -\alpha} - 1/3)}\right)^2 w^2(\mc{T}). \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (negative result)
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to maximizing $\langle \Pi\epsilon, u\rangle$ and construct a sign-matching permutation $\Pi_\pm$. Concentration of $\sum|g_i||h_i|$, Hoeffding and singular value bounds give the lower bound.

nodes.name: Reformulate via radial parametrization
nodes.statement: Consider the least squares problem \eqref{eq:lsq} with $\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol{\epsilon}$: \begin{equation*} \min_{\Pi, \beta} \nnorm{\boldsymbol{\epsilon} - \Pi X \beta}_2^2. \end{equation*} Omitting the term not depending on $\beta$, an equivalent problem is given by \begin{equation*} \min_{\Pi, \beta} -2 \scp{\Pi \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{X \beta} + \nnorm{X \beta}_2^2. \end{equation*} Re-parameterizing $X \beta = u \cdot r$, with $r \geq 0$ for $u \in \text{range}(X) \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$, we obtain the optimization problem \begin{equation*} \min_{\Pi, u \in \text{range}(X) \cap \mathbb{S}^{n-1}, r \geq 0} -2 \scp{\Pi \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{u} r + r^2. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite least squares with pure noise as an optimization over a direction $u$ and radius $r$.

nodes.name: Optimal radius
nodes.statement: Observe that for any $u$ and $\Pi$, the optimal value of $r$ is found as \begin{equation*} \wh{r}(u) = \max\{\scp{\Pi \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{u},0 \}. \end{equation*} In particular, for a minimizer $(\wh{\Pi}, \wh{u})$, \begin{equation*} \wh{r} \coloneq \wh{r}(\wh{\Pi}, \wh{u}) = \nscp{\wh{\Pi} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{\wh{u}} \end{equation*} so that $\wh{r} = \nnorm{X \wh{\beta}}_2$, and the optimal value of the objective is given by $-\wh{r}^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Optimal $r$ equals the inner product, so $\hat r=\|X\hat\beta\|_2$.

nodes.name: Lower bound by first column
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound $\hat r$ by the best permutation against the first column $X_1$.

nodes.name: Construct sign-matching permutation
nodes.statement_short: Construct $\Pi_\pm$ pairing signs of $\epsilon$ and $X_1$.

nodes.name: Counts of sign-matched indices
nodes.statement: n_+ = \min\{n_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon},+}, n_{X_1,+} \}, \quad n_- = \min\{n_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon},-}, n_{X_1,-} \}, \quad n_{\pm} = n - n_+ - n_-.
nodes.label: eq:nplusnminus

nodes.name: Distribution and expectation of the matched sum
nodes.statement: All terms inside the first two sums are i.i.d.~from the same distribution as $|g| |h|$, where $g$ and $h$ are independent $N(0,1)$-random variables, and accordingly the terms inside the last summand are i.i.d.~from the same distribution as $-|g||h|$. Conditional on $n_{\pm}$, hence $\nscp{\Pi_{\pm} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{X_1}$ follows the same distribution as \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} |g_i| |h_i| - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} |g_i| |h_i|, \end{equation*} where $\{ g_i \}_{i = 1}^n$ and $\{ h_i \}_{i = 1}^n$ are two independent sequences of $n$ i.i.d.~random variables from the $N(0,1)$-distribution. The expectation of the above expression (conditional on $n_{\pm}$) is given by \begin{equation*} (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \E[|g||h|] = (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \E[|g|]^2 = (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \frac{2}{\pi}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Matched sum is distributed as a difference of sums of $|g||h|$ with mean $(n-2n_\pm)2/\pi$.

nodes.name: Concentration inequality
nodes.statement: From Proposition 5.16 in \cite{Vershynin2010}, we have the following concentration inequality: \begin{equation*} \p \left(\left|\sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} (|g_i| |h_i| - \E[|g||h|]) - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} (|g_i| |h_i| - \E[|g||h|]) \right| \geq (n - 2 n_{\pm}) \frac{1}{\pi} \Big| n_{\pm} \right) \leq \exp(-n c). \end{equation*} Hence, conditional on $n_{\pm}$, with probability at least $1 - \exp(-nc)$, \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} |g_i| |h_i| - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} |g_i| |h_i| \geq \frac{1}{\pi} (n - 2 n_{\pm}). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Apply sub-exponential concentration (Vershynin Prop. 5.16).

nodes.name: Control $n_\pm$ via Hoeffding
nodes.statement: Consider the definition of $n_+$ and $n_-$ Observe that $n_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, +}$, $n_{X_1, +}$, $n_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, -}$ and $n_{X_1, -}$ are each binomial random variables with $n$ trials and probability of success $1/2$. By repeated application of Hoeffding's inequality, we hence have \begin{equation*} \p(n_{+} \leq 3n/8) \leq 2\exp(-n/32), \quad \p(n_{-} \leq 3n/8) \leq 2 \exp(-n/32). \end{equation*} Conditional on the events $\{ n_{+} > 3n/8\}$ and $\{ n_{-} > 3n/8\}$, we have $n_{\pm} \leq 1/4$ and thus with probability at least $1 - C \exp(-nc)$ \begin{equation*} \sum_{i = 1}^{n - n_{\pm}} |g_i| |h_i| - \sum_{i=n - n_{\pm} + 1}^{n} |g_i| |h_i| \geq \frac{n}{2\pi} . \end{equation*} Accordingly, the same applies to the event $\{ \nscp{\Pi_{\pm} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{X_1} > \frac{n}{2\pi} \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hoeffding bounds $n_+, n_-$, giving $\langle\Pi_\pm\epsilon,X_1\rangle > n/(2\pi)$ w.h.p.

nodes.name: Bound column norm
nodes.statement_short: Norm concentration bounds $\|X_1\|_2$, yielding a lower bound on $\|X\hat\beta\|_2$.

nodes.name: Conclude with singular value bound
nodes.statement: Finally, Lemma \ref{lem:extremesingularvalues} in Appendix \ref{app:aux} yields that $\sigma_{\max}(X) \leq \sqrt{2n} + \sqrt{d}$ with probability at least $1 - \exp(-c n)$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\sigma_{\max}(X)$ to convert into a lower bound on $\|\hat\beta\|_2$.

nodes.statement_short: Decouple $\hat\Pi$ and $\hat\beta$, bound $\|(\hat\Pi^T-\Pi^{*T})y\|_2$ via Gordon's escape theorem, then plug into the OLS expansion.

nodes.statement: We start with a basic, yet important observation that allows us to decouple $\wh{\Pi}$ and $\wh{\beta}$. Let $\texttt{P}_X$ and $\texttt{P}_X^{\perp}$ denote the orthogonal projection on $\text{range}(X)$ respectively its orthogonal complement.

Then, if $n \geq d$, with probability one \begin{equation} \wh{\Pi}^{\T} \in \argmin_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \nnorm{\emph{\texttt{P}}_X^{\perp} \Pi \mathbf{y}}_2^2, \qquad \wh{\beta} \in \left\{ \left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-1} \frac{X^{\T} \wh{\Pi}^{\T} \mathbf{y}}{n}, \; \, \wh{\Pi}^{\T} \in \argmin_{\Pi \in \mc{P}_{n,k}} \nnorm{\emph{\texttt{P}}_X^{\perp} \Pi \mathbf{y}}_2^2 \right \}. \end{equation} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} We have \begin{align*} \min_{\Pi, \beta} \|\Pi X\beta-\mathbf{y}\|_2^2 &= \min_{\Pi, \beta} \|X\beta-\Pi \mathbf{y}\|_2^2 \\ &= \min_{\Pi, \beta} \left\{ \|\texttt{P}_X^{\perp} \Pi \mathbf{y}\|_2^2 + \|X\beta- \texttt{P}_X \Pi \mathbf{y}\|_2^2 \right\}. \end{align*} The second part can always be made equal to zero by choosing $\beta$ such that $X \beta = \texttt{P}_X \Pi \mathbf{y}$. nodes.name: Separation lemma
nodes.statement: The proof of part (a) of the theorem relies on two lemmas, which are stated and proved first. \begin{lemma} Let $\gamma, \delta > 0$. Consider the event \begin{equation} \mathcal{A}_{\gamma}= \left\{\min_{i<j}(\mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta^*-\mathbf{x}_j^\top\beta^*)^2\le \gamma^2 \right\}. \end{equation} Then $\p\left( \mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\right)< \delta$ if \[ \nnorm{\beta^*}_2^2>\dfrac{n^2(n-1)^2}{4\delta^2\pi}\gamma^2. \] \end{lemma} \begin{proof} It is clear that $\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\subseteq\bigcup_{i<j}\left\{(\mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta^*-\mathbf{x}_j^\top\beta^*)^2\le \gamma^2 \right\}$. Using the fact that $\mathbf{x}_i^\top\beta^*-\mathbf{x}_j^\top\beta^*\sim N(0,2\|\beta^*\|_2^2)$, we have \begin{align*} \p\left(\mathcal{A}_{\gamma}\right)&\le\p\left(\bigcup_{i<j}\left\{-\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2}\le (\mathbf{x}_i -\mathbf{x}_j)^\top\dfrac{\beta^*}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2}\le \dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2}\right\}\right) \\ &\le \sum_{i<j}\p\left( -\dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2} \le g \leq \dfrac{\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\|\beta^*\|_2} \right), \quad g \sim N(0,1)\\ &\le\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \dfrac{\gamma}{\|\beta^*\|_2\sqrt{\pi}} \quad \text{by Lemma \ref{lem:smallball} in Appendix \ref{app:aux}.} \end{align*} Thus, it suffices to require that $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} \dfrac{\gamma}{\|\beta^*\|_2\sqrt{\pi}}<\delta$. nodes.statement: We invoke Lemma \ref{lem:hansonwright} conditional on $X$, with $\left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-1} \frac{X^{\T}}{\sqrt{n}}$ in the role of $A$, so that $\Gamma = \frac{X}{\sqrt{n}} \left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-2} \frac{X^{\T}}{\sqrt{n}}$. Observe that \begin{align} \begin{split} &(i)\;\;\mathrm{tr}(\Gamma) = \mathrm{tr}\left( \left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-1} \right) \leq \frac{d}{\sigma^2_{\min}(X / \sqrt{n})}, \quad (ii) \;\; \nnorm{\Gamma}_2 = \frac{1}{\sigma^2_{\min}(X / \sqrt{n})}, \\ &(iii)\;\;\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\Gamma^2)} = \sqrt{\mathrm{tr} \left(\left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-2} \right)} \leq \frac{\sqrt{d}}{\sigma^2_{\min}(X/\sqrt{n})}. \end{split} \end{align} In view of the relations in \eqref{eq:traceineq}, application of Lemma \ref{lem:hansonwright} with $t = d \vee \log n$ and comparison of terms yields that \begin{equation*} \p\left(\norm{ \left(\frac{X^{\T} X}{n} \right)^{-1} \frac{X^{\T} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}{\sqrt{n}}}_2 \; > \sigma \frac{\sqrt{5 \{d \vee \log n \}}}{\sigma_{\min}(X / \sqrt{n})} \; \; \Bigg| X \right) \leq \exp(-d \vee \log n). \end{equation*} Using Lemma \ref{lem:extremesingularvalues} for $\sigma_{\min}(X)$ with the choice $t = \sqrt{d \vee \log n}$, the assertion readily follows.
nodes.statement_short: Hanson-Wright conditional on $X$ plus extreme singular value concentration.

nodes.name: Concentration of Gaussian processes
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Concentration of Gaussian processes \cite{Boucheron2013}})} Let $K$ be a closed subset of the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with Gaussian width $w(K)$, and let $g \sim N(0, I_m)$. Then for all $t > 0$ \begin{equation*} \p \left(\sup_{x \in K} |\scp{g}{x}| \geq w(K) + t \right) \leq \exp(-t^2/2). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $K$ be a closed subset of the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with Gaussian width $w(K)$, and let $g \sim N(0, I_m)$.
nodes.label: lem:concentration_width

nodes.name: Concentration of the norm of Gaussian random vectors
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Concentration of the norm of Gaussian random vectors \cite{Vershynin2010}})}\\ Let $g \sim N(0, I_n)$. Then for all $t > 0$, $\p(\nnorm{g}_2 \geq (1 + t) \sqrt{n}) \leq \exp(-t^2 n / 2)$.
nodes.label: lem:normconcentration

nodes.name: Concentration of extreme singular values of Gaussian matrices
nodes.statement: \hspace*{-.7ex}\emph{(\textbf{Concentration of extreme singular values of Gaussian matrices \cite{Vershynin2010}})}\\ Let $X$ be an $n \times d$ Gaussian matrix with i.i.d.~$N(0,1)$-entries. Denote by $\sigma_{\min}(X)$ and $\sigma_{\max}(X)$ the minimum respectively maximum singular value of $X$. Then for any $t > 0$ \begin{equation*} \p(\sigma_{\min}(X) \geq \sqrt{n} - \sqrt{d} - t) \leq \exp(-t^2 / 2), \qquad \p(\sigma_{\max}(X) \geq \sqrt{n} + \sqrt{d} + t) \leq \exp(-t^2 / 2). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $X$ be an $n \times d$ Gaussian matrix with i.i.d.~$N(0,1)$-entries.
nodes.label: lem:extremesingularvalues

nodes.name: Concentration of quadratic forms (Hanson-Wright type)
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Concentration of quadratic forms \cite{Hsu2012}})}\\ Let $A$ be a an $m \times n$ matrix, $\Gamma = A^{\T} A$, and $g \sim N(0, I_n)$. Then for all $t > 0$ \begin{equation*} \p(\nnorm{A g}_2^2 > \mathrm{tr}(\Gamma) + 2 \sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\Gamma^2) t} + 2 \nnorm{\Gamma}_2 t) \leq \exp(-t). \end{equation*}
assumptions: Let $A$ be a an $m \times n$ matrix, $\Gamma = A^{\T} A$, and $g \sim N(0, I_n)$.
nodes.label: lem:hansonwright

nodes.name: Maximal inequality for Gaussian random variables
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Maximal inequality for Gaussian random variables})}\\ Let $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ be zero-mean Gaussian random variables such that $\max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \E[g_i^2] \leq \sigma^2$. Then for all $M > 0$, $\p(\max_{1 \leq i \leq n} |g_i| > (1+M) \sigma \sqrt{2 \log n}) \leq 2n^{-M^2}$.
assumptions: Let $g_1, \ldots, g_n$ be zero-mean Gaussian random variables such that $\max_{1 \leq i \leq n} \E[g_i^2] \leq \sigma^2$.
nodes.label: lem:maximalgaussian

nodes.name: Small ball probability
nodes.statement: \emph{(\textbf{Small ball probability})}\\ Let $g \sim N(0,1)$. Then for all $t > 0$, $\p(|g| < t) \leq \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \, t < t$.
nodes.label: lem:smallball
